newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW-Mexico's Bufete sees sales surge.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Mexico's Bufete sees sales surge.

text.p: The head of Mexican construction giant Bufete Industrial SA de CV expects sales to surge in 1997 as the government pumps long-awaited investment into giant infrastructure projects such as boosting oil production.

In a rare recent interview, Bufete's 72-year-old magnate Jose Mendoza Fernandez said total sales this year are expected to grow more than 45 percent in real terms compared with 1995, up from real growth of 33 percent in the first nine months.
"In 1997, the projections are that we could grow 10 to 15 percent in real terms compared with 1996. That's very important growth," Mendoza added.

Though building firms were among the hardest hit by Mexico's biting 1995 recession, Bufete did $1.4 billion of business between April 1995 and March 1996 -- a feat that still makes Mendoza's eyes light up. He said Bufete weathered the crisis by building for corporations savvy enough to see investment opportunities where others saw crisis. That meant switching to private sector clients from its previous main contractor -- the government.

"Up to 1994, Bufete worked from 75 or 80 percent for the public sector...In 1995 and so far in 1996, it's turned around. Now we have 75 percent of private contracts and 25 percent in the public sector," he said. Though he expects Bufete to still do at least 50 percent of its work for private firms, next year he expects government contracts to rebound.

One of his main hopes for growth next year is the government's stated intention to boost public investment. He said state oil giant Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) has some $5 billion earmarked next year for projects such as boosting crude oil production in the Cantarell field, near Campeche.

Government officials on Monday put the energy investment budget at 68.697 billion pesos ($8.7 billion) in 1997. Hopes that contracts would rain Bufete's way sent its stock soaring on Tuesday in Mexican and New York markets, analysts said.

"Next year, we're going to have what we haven't had in many years, such as important investments in Pemex, important tenders for the Federal Electricity Commission, and all the privatization plans via public service concessions," Mendoza said, explaining where Bufete's growth would come from.
The oil production contracts, he said, would be offered and completed next year.
On the other hand, a $1.2 billion tender offer for expanding refining capacity in Cadereyta, Nuevo Leon, would probably not pay dividends until 1998, he added.

Bufete is in talks with its main Mexican rival Empresas ICA to jointly tender for the Cadereyta contract, he said. In bidding for a huge power plant contract, Merida III, it has formed a consortium with Enron Corp, ABB and Black and Veatch.

Mendoza welcomed the government's decision in October to limit the sale of Pemex' secondary petrochemical plants to joint government-private sector ventures, saying that the legal framework for selling off the plants for 100 percent private ownership was fuzzy. He acknowledged that the decision caused some discontent, however.

Under the new plan, in which the government has defined which nine petrochemicals it has the exclusive right to exploit, there should be an influx of firms who want to build fully-owned plants, Mendoza said.

"That's why Shell (Royal Dutch/Shell Group) has already come in and set up its PET (polyethelene terephthalate) plant (in Tampico). Eastman (Chemical Co) did the same (in Veracruz). The wise guys who are looking long term have already got a head start," he said.
